LESSON 5 OF 12·Injection, XSS & Client-Side Defenses

SQL Injection & Parameterized Queries

Understand how string concatenation turns user input into database commands, and why prepared statements keep code and data separate.

Beginner24 min
Why this matters

SQL injection (SQLi) occurs when an application builds a database query by concatenating untrusted input directly into the SQL command string. Because the database parser cannot tell where the developer’s query ends and the user’s data begins, crafted characters can alter query logic, bypass checks, read unauthorized rows, or modify data. The primary defense is structural: parameterized queries (prepared statements) compile the SQL structure first and pass user values separately as bound parameters.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

Architecture & Trust Boundary Flow

How untrusted input crosses into an interpreter — and how parameterization separates code from data.

  1. Input: Caller supplies a search term or record filter in the HTTP request.
  2. Boundary: Application binds the value to an expected query structure.
  3. Result: Database returns only rows matching the intended predicate.
01 Crafted Payload

02 String Concatenation
Unblocked

  1. Input: Input includes SQL syntax tokens (quotes, operators, or UNION clauses).
  2. Boundary: Concatenation merges untrusted characters directly into the command string.
  3. Result: Database parser interprets user data as instructions, bypassing filters.
01 Untrusted Input
Typed parameter
02 Prepared Statement (?)
Verified
03 Bound Execution
  1. Input: Any string—even containing quotes or SQL keywords—arrives at the handler.
  2. Boundary: Database compiles the SQL statement tree before binding parameters as literal scalars.
  3. Result: Payload is treated strictly as inert data; query structure cannot change.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • An application receives input from a query parameter, form field, header, cookie, or stored record.
  • If the code concatenates that input into a raw SQL string, characters like quotes, operators, or SQL keywords are parsed as part of the command syntax.
  • In-band SQLi returns results directly in the page; blind SQLi infers answers from boolean page differences or database response delays.
  • With a parameterized query, the database compiles the statement template ahead of time and treats the bound parameter strictly as a literal value, never as executable SQL syntax.

The background

First documented widely in Phrack Magazine in 1998, SQL injection has remained one of the most damaging web vulnerability classes for over two decades despite having a clear, universal engineering fix.

Real-world examples

  • High-profile breaches have repeatedly traced back to legacy endpoints or dynamic ORDER BY / filter clauses where developers bypassed query parameterization.
  • Even modern ORM frameworks can expose SQL injection when raw query helpers or string interpolation are used for dynamic table or column names.

What to look for

  • Search codebases for string interpolation or concatenation inside SQL query builders and raw ORM query calls.
  • Check dynamic sorting, filtering, and search endpoints where column names or directions cannot use standard value placeholders.
  • Verify that database error messages and stack traces are logged internally rather than returned in HTTP responses.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Use parameterized queries (prepared statements) for every variable data value in SQL statements.
  • Validate dynamic identifiers such as column names or sort orders against a strict server-side allowlist.
  • Run the application database connection with least-privilege credentials limited to required tables and operations.
  • Avoid exposing raw database driver errors to clients.
